Syngas Production from Electrocatalytic CO2 Reduction with High Energetic Efficiency and Current Density Ping Chen,a,b Yan Jiao,†a Yi-Han Zhu,†c Shuang-Ming Chen,d Li Song,d Mietek Jaroniec,e Yao Zheng,*a Shi-Zhang Qiao*a,f
The direct conversion from CO2 to syngas with controllable composition remains of intense interest for the production of renewable fuels. Large current density as well as high cell voltage efficiency are critical from practical viewpoint for electrochemical CO2 reduction reaction (CRR) while the design of catalysts is a great challenge. Here we report the oxidederived Cu nanowires with abundant amount of highly dispersed two-phase CuO heterostructure for syngas generation. The specified H2/CO ratios of 1, 2 and 3 with extra high CRR Faradic efficiency (90 %) and energetic efficiency (50 %) were achieved. The density functional theory calculations reveal that the misfit dislocation sites in the electrocatalyst break the inherent scaling relationship of CRR intermediates’ adsorption energy with an extraordinarily strong adsorption of *COOH, and consequently promote an excellent activity of the catalyst toward CRR. Driven by a commercial solar cell (working voltage of 2.2 V) under direct sunlight, the freestanding electrocatalyst can steadily generate syngas of the desired composition using CO2 as a feedstock.

sections.heading: Broader context
sections.text: Syngas (CO/H2) is a key platform for chemical utilization of nonpetroleum carbon resources. The syngas with H2/CO ratio of 1 can be used for hydroformylation of alkenes to aldehydes. The syngas with H2/CO ratio of 2 is suited for methanol synthesis or Fischer-Tropsch processes, which is widely employed in industries to produce various liquid fuels. The syngas with H2/CO ratios of 3 is ideal for the methane synthesis reaction. Controllable syngas production with high energetic efficiency and current density from electrocatalytic CO2 reduction is critical but still very challenging. Here, the specified H2/CO ratios of 1, 2 and 3 were generated on the oxide-derived Cu nanowires electrode. This work realizes the controlled syngas production using a solar cell drived by direct sunlight radiation and CO2 as a feedstock.

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.text:
Electrochemical conversion of CO2 into fuels and chemicals is a promising strategy for high-density renewable energy storage. Because of the high reaction barrier and inevitable hydrogen evolution reaction (HER) competition, the CO2 reduction reaction (CRR) to carbonaceous products is slow and needs a high overpotential to proceed.1,2 These two issues largely restrain the possibility of coupling the electrochemical conversion of CO2 with some renewable energy input such as solar cells to deliver an acceptable cell voltage efficiency. Apparently, a high energy efficiency (E.E., collectively determined by a low overpotential and a high Faradaic efficiency, F.E.) and large partial current density for a certain product are the paramount parameters for the practical operation of electrochemical CO2 conversion.3 The design of highly active and selective electrocatalysts for CRR is critical to achieve these targets but still very challenging.4
CO is one of the most common and important products of CO2 reduction. By coupling it with water splitting, an electrochemical co-production of H2 and CO is achievable via a combination of HER and CRR processes. Various types of syngas with tunable H2/CO ratio (e.g., 1, 2, and 3) are the key feedstock components for industrial-scale production of liquid fuels and chemicals. Currently, syngas is most often generated by the steam reforming of natural gas with large carbon footprint. Limited success has been achieved toward clean syngas

production associated with renewable energy and by using abundant CO2 as a feedstock.5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10, 11 One of the most important reasons is that E.E. of the electrocatalytic CRR is still unsatisfactory. So far, a range of highly selective electrocatalysts for conversion CO2 to CO with F.E. exceeding 90 % and electrocatalytically active HER electrocatalysts have been developed individually.12, 13, 14 However, to achieve a tunable H2/CO ratio, a delicate balance between CRR and HER on one surface is essential. A possible solution is the rational design of electrocatalysts with one (or two) appropriate catalytic site(s) for the generation of a series of key reaction intermediates of CRR and HER.15 Moreover, to achieve high E.E. as well as current density at the same time to make the production process feasible, a well-designed physical structure of the electrocatalyst with exposed sufficient number of active sites is indispensable.
Up to now, metallic Cu is the most well understood electrocatalyst for CRR, from both experimental and theoretical viewpoints.16 Also, Cu can generate CO and H2 coherently at different rates, depending on the applied potentials.1 However, other carbonaceous products (ethylene, methane, formate, etc.) are also generated under the same potentials, yielding a maximum CO F.E. of ~40 % (excluding H2).1 From an experimental viewpoint, it has proved very difficult to increase the CO selectivity on a single Cu site due to the inherent scaling of adsorption energies for different intermediates (to be specific, *COOH, *CO, *CHO, etc.).12 This scaling relationship also fundamentally limits the activity of an electrocatalyst (in terms of the overpotential for generation of one type of species) to reach the theoretically maximum value.17 As a result, even though substantial progress has been made to develop Cubased electrocatalysts for efficient CRR, a large negative potential (e.g., -0.6 V vs. reversible hydrogen electrode, RHE) is still needed to achieve a favorable CO F.E. (for instance >80 %).18, 19, 20, 21 Therefore, high overall F.E., and more importantly, high E.E. of CO generation is still challenging. Even though some precious metal electrocatalysts with relatively weak *CO intermediate adsorption can produce gaseous CO with F.E. exceeding 90 % at low overpotentials, the HER rates on these surfaces are always slow due to the very weak *H intermediate adsorption. An electrocatalyst for high performance syngas production is still missing to suit the requirements for practical applications.
Here, we propose an atomically dispersed heterostructure of CuO on the freestanding Cu nanowires (CuNWs) as highly effective electrocatalyst for CO2 conversion to syngas due to an extraordinarily strong adsorption of reaction intermediate *COOH on its surface. Consequently, a fast kinetic CO generation with low overpotential and high partial current density were achieved on the misfit dislocation sites present on the surface of CuNWs. By subtle tuning the water splitting reaction rate on this electrocatalyst, the desired composition of syngas with the H2/CO ratio of 1, 2 or 3) can be achieved with very high energetic efficiency of ~50 % as well as high current density of ~5.0 mA/cm2 at low overpotential, outperforming the
most of reported Cu-family electrocatalysts. For the first time, by combining this electrocatalytic system with a commercial solar cell panel (working voltage of 2.2 V) and using CO2 as a feedstock, a stable rate of ~7 µmol/min/gcatal of H2/CO = 2 syngas can be generated under a direct sunlight illumination.

The highly crystalline Cu nanowires (Cu NWs) were synthesized via a reduction method in aqueous phase.22 The freshly produced Cu NWs were subjected to continuous air-oxidation under ambient conditions, high temperature oxidation (300- 400 oC), then in-situ electrochemical reduction under aqueous conditions (Fig. 1a, Fig. S1). As compared to pristine Cu, the reduced samples at different temperatures (300, 350 and 400 oC), denoted as r-Cuox(300), r-Cuox(350) and r-Cuox(400), show similar rod-like morphology but with abundant outgrowths on their surfaces (Fig. 1b,c, Fig. S2a,b). These outgrowths may be formed due to adsorption of water molecules from air in the first oxidization process, which etched the surface of Cu NWs in the second high temperature oxidization process. The X-ray diffraction (XRD) profiles (Fig. 1d) show that pristine Cu has a clear face-centered cubic (f.c.c.) crystal structure, while rCuox(350) shows both cubic phase CuO (c-CuO) and monoclinic CuO (m-CuO) phase in the structure in addition to metallic Cu. These results are also consistent with X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) and synchrotron-based X-ray absorption near edge structure (XANES) data that are more surface sensitive. The high resolution XPS spectra of r-Cuox(350) show more Cu2+ species than those on pristine Cu (Fig. 1e). The XANES spectra also show that there is an obvious energy shift to the higher energy (i.e., higher valance states) of Cu K-edge in rCuox(350) in comparison to pristine Cu (Fig. 1f). Moreover, the Fourier transform r-space of extended X-ray absorption fine structure (EXAFS) shows that besides Cu-Cu main peak, there is a certain amount of Cu-O species on the r-Cuox(350) surface (Fig. 1g). The fitting results also show the coordination number of Cu in r-Cuox(350) is lower than those in the pristine Cu and Cu foil references (Table S1).
Heterostructure Identification
As can be seen from the scanning transmission electron microscopy (STEM) image (Figure S3 in the supporting information), there are some outgrowths on the surface of rCuox(350). The corresponding elemental mapping indicate there are some oxygen species in these structures. From the lowmagnification TEM image, each Cu NW is covered by a thick shell with irregular outgrowths (Fig. 2a inset). Electron diffraction pattern allows an explicit identification of polycrystalline nature of the shell enclosure, of which the radially integrated profile can be perfectly indexed by m-CuO, cCuO and bulk Cu phases, as similarly observed by XRD and XPS analysis (Fig. 2b). High-resolution TEM image provides atomic level structures of the outer polycrystalline shells, which are made of mixed CuO domains with different crystal structures and orientations (Fig. 2a). Specifically, an m-CuO domain with rhombic lattice (shown by green dashed rectangle in panel a) can be identified on the HRTEM image and the indexed FFT along its [010] direction, where two reciprocal vectors [002]* and [200]* have an angle of ~81o (Fig. 2c-e). Another domain with a square lattice (shown by yellow dashed rectangle in panel a) can be similarly identified as c-CuO structure, which is a metastable phase with a face-centred lattice (Fig. 2f-h). Noted that the c-CuO structure has a very similar cell with previously reported Cu2O phase.23, 24, 25 However, the absence of (110)
reflections in the FFT arising from the face-centering of the cCuO structure allows us to exclude the Cu2O structure (Fig. 2g), of which the oxygen sublattice breaks such lattice-centering. Interestingly, the intergrown domains of m-CuO and c-CuO heterostructures with an orientation relationship of {001}<010>c-CuO//{001}<010>m-CuO is visible (shown in red dashed rectangles in panel a), where two sets of reflections are superimposed in the FFT as shown in Fig. 2j. These two types of nanometer-sized domains are highly strained and interpenetrated, where misfit dislocations were formed at the interface of the heterostructure (see the interfacial structural model as shown in Fig. 2k). One can speculate that the intergrown m-CuO/c-CuO heterostructure may originate from the phase transition between these two structures during the oxidation-reduction processes of r-Cuox(350).
Figure 2. (a,b) TEM and HRTEM images of a randomly chosen r-Cuox(350) NW. (b) Electron
diffraction pattern and corresponding radially-integrated profile (inset) for r-Cuox(350) NW. Black, white and red indices refer to m-CuO, c-CuO and Cu phases, respectively. (c) HRTEM image, (d) FFT pattern and (e) projected structural model of the region marked by green dashed rectangle in panel a. (f) HRTEM image, (g) FFT pattern and (h) projected structural model of the region marked by yellow dashed rectangle in panel a. (i) HRTEM image of intergrown domains of m-CuO and c-CuO indicated by red dashed rectangles in panel b. (j) FFT pattern and (k) corresponding structural model. Green and yellow rectangles in panel j are used to mark the reciprocal lattices of m-CuO and c-CuO, respectively. Color code in the structural models: blue, copper; red, oxygen.

Cuox samples for CRR performance. As expected, all freshly reduced electrodes show slightly higher overall current density and lower overpotential than pristine Cu (Fig. 3a, Fig. S4a). Additionally, the reduced samples with oxide species show higher F.E. of carbonaceous products (mainly CO) than the pristine one (Fig. 3b, Fig. S4-S6). Taking the best performing rCuox(350) as an example, CO starts to generate at as low as -0.30 V vs RHE (~0.20 V overpotential) and reaches a maximum F.E. of 48 % at -0.49 V vs RHE (Fig. 3b). These values are better than the values for the most of reported Cu-based CO generating electrocatalysts.21, 24, 26, 27, 28 Conversely, the F.E. of CO on the pristine Cu was lower than 10 % with very strong HER competition in the entire testing range (Fig. S5). Note that for the r-Cuox(350) electrode H2 and CO are the major gaseous products detected in the range of -0.15 to -0.70 V (see Fig. 3b). There are also some C2H4 and C2H6 species confirmed as mpurities from CO2 reactant. The liquid product contains a small amount of HCOO- and no deep reduction products are detected, e.g., C2H5OH. The double layer capacitance (DLC) obtained by cyclic voltammetry (CV) was adopted to evaluate the electrochemically active surface area. Fig. S7 shows the CVs of the pristine Cu, r-Cuox(300), r-Cuox(350) and r-Cuox(400) catalysts in the potential range, in which Faradaic processes are not occurring in 0.1 M KHCO3 electrolyte. According to the approximate linear relationship of the geometric current density against the scan rate of CVs, the pristine Cu, r-Cuox(300), r-Cuox(350) and r-Cuox(400) show the capacitance of 34.25, 81.65, 102.50 and 84.35 mF.cm-2, respectively. Among all the samples, the r-Cuox(350) has the maximum capacitance, which may contribute in part to its best performance.
Figure 3. Electrochemical performance of CO2 reduction in a three-electrode system. (a) Polarization curves of r-Cuox(350) and pristine Cu catalysts in CO2-satuated 0.1 M KHCO3 solution. (b) F.E. of CO, H2 and HCOOH products as a function of potential for r-Cuox(350). (c) Molar rate of H2 to CO products as a function of the potential for r-Cuox(350). (d) E.E. of CO, H2 and overall products as a function of the potential for r-Cuox(350).
More interestingly, the molar ratio of H2 to CO depends strongly on the applied potential and can be controlled exactly from 3 to 1 (Fig. 3c). For example, at an applied potential of -0.39 V vs RHE (i.e., overpotential of 0.28 V and 0.39 V for CO and H2 generation, respectively), r-Cuox(350) delivers a very high current density (~5.0 mA/cm2) precisely with the molar ratio of H2/CO = 2.0 that is well suited for direct methanol synthesis. Importantly, the overall E.E for the entire range of syngas mixtures is always ~50 % due to the low generation overpotentials and high F.E. (Fig. 3d). These exceptional E.E. and cathodic current density values of the newly developed r-
Cuox(350), which are the two key indexes for the aforementioned industrial application of CO2 conversion technology, are much higher than those reported for other Cubased CRR electrocatalysts for various types of syngas generation (Fig. S8, Table S2).5, 9, 10, 11, 18, 20, 24, 27, 28

sections.heading: Catalytic Mechanisms
sections.text:
It is well known that the reduction of CuO, either in-situ or exsitu, can introduce a range of different types of defects on the lattice of derived Cu (e.g. grain boundaries), which are electrocatalytically active for CO2 and CO reductions.21, 24, 29, 30 We also noticed a distinctive adsorption behavior of OH- as compared to pristine Cu. As shown in Fig. 4a, besides regular redox peaks from facets of metallic Cu itself, there is an extra shoulder on the r-Cuox(350) surface under negative potentials, which indicates stronger OH- interactions in the case of the rCuox(350) surface than pristine Cu.21 We attribute these features to the presence of oxide species in r-Cuox(350). Such stronger OH- interactions on r-Cuox(350) can not only surpass the competing HER due to the increased local pH value slowing the kinetics of the first water reduction step (the Volmer step),31 but also can increase the kinetics of CRR by enhancing the adsorption ability of *COOH reaction intermediate.32
Figure 4. Mechanistic study of syngas generation on r-Cuox(350) catalyst. (a) CVs of rCuox(350) and pristine Cu catalysts in N2-satuated 0.1 M KOH solution; arrows show adsorption of additional OH- species. (b) Partial current of CO and H2 as a function of the potential for r-Cuox(350) catalyst. (c,d) Partial current of CO and H2 for r-Cuox(350) catalyst under different concentrations of CO2-satuated KHCO3 solutions.
Interestingly, for r-Cuox(350) electrocatalyst under CRR conditions, the partial current of hydrogen generation increases constantly with increasing overpotential, while the CO generation reaches a plateau at a certain overpotential (Fig. 4b,c). This can be assigned to the limited CO2 mass transport in the electrolyte at high CO generation rate.6 Consequently, the appropriate HER and CRR rates deliver a controllable molar ratio of H2 and CO to form various types of syngas under different potentials (Fig. 3c). Also, the CO generation rate on r-Cuox(350) decreases with increasing HCO3- concentration (Fig. 4c, Fig. S9). This is partly attributed to the rate change of competing HER, but more importantly is from the mechanistic perspective.33 It is known that the initial proton donation for CO2 reduction originates from HCO3- in the solution; a dependence of the HCO3- concentration on the reaction rate indicates that the hydrogenation step is the rate determining step (RDS), while an independence trend indicates the single electron transfer to CO2 is RDS.34, 35. Such very small or even negative rate order of HCO3- toward CO formation on r-Cuox(350) indicates electron transfer to CO2 as RDS, which is consistent with other very active and selective CO generation materials like Au and Ag, where the rate value is close to zero.36, 37

sections.heading: Origin of Heterostructure Activity
sections.text:
To explain the origin of exceptional CRR activity of the rCuox(350) surface at atomic level, the reaction free energy diagrams of CO and H2 evolution were obtained for different structures (Fig. 5a,b). Crystallographic planes for the investigated models (m-CuO(010), c-CuO(001), and CuOheterostructure as shown in Fig. S10) were selected based on the experimental HRTEM results outlined in Fig. 2. The Cu(111) surface was also considered to simulate the pristine Cu for the purpose of comparison (Fig. S11). As shown in Fig. S11-S14, CO2 molecules chemisorb at the heterojunction of m-CuO and c-CuO with an adsorption energy of -0.45 eV, much more negative than those on the Cu(111) and c-CuO surfaces. Due to the experimental evidence that the initial electron transfer is the RDS for CRR, a strong CO2 adsorption may benefit the subsequent activation and reduction processes. As regards the CRR pathway, the CuO-heterostructure is the most energetically favorable one among all four surfaces with the free energy of 0.31 eV for CO2 progression to *COOH intermediate state (Fig. 5a, Fig. S15-S18). The only other thermodynamically uphill step (0.26 eV free energy change) on this surface is desorption of *CO to gaseous CO product. On the other hand, the Cu(111) surface shows the best theoretical HER activity due to its smallest hydrogen adsorption free energy (∆GH) value (Fig. 5b, Fig. S19); all CuO structures possess stronger hydrogen adsorption abilities that lead to a worse HER selectivity. These theoretical considerations are in good agreement with experimental observation that the HER rates on the synthesized r-Cuox samples with oxide species are much lower than that on the pristine Cu (Fig. 3b, Fig. S8).
The underlying reason for CuO-heterostructure possessing much enhanced CRR activity (in terms of limiting potential) toward CO product is that the intrinsic scaling relationship between *COOH and *CO reaction intermediates’ adsorption energy is broken. As shown in Fig. 5a, the overall activity of the CO2 reduction to CO is thermodynamically controlled by the free energy change of three steps: *COOH formation, *CO formation and *CO desorption. It is well known that there is a liner scaling relationship between the adsorption energies of
*COOH and *CO on a range of metal surfaces, identified in Fig. 5c as a 2D volcano-shaped activity map. As can be clearly seen, this inherent scaling relationship confines the pure metal materials from the activity peak (the deep red area in Fig. 5c).38, 39, 40, 41 However, for the interface of CuO-heterostructure, it is closer to reach the volcano peak by deviating from the linear relationship with a stronger *COOH adsorption and a similar *CO adsorption as in the case of the Cu(111) surface. This enhanced *COOH adsorption on the CuO-heterostructure can be attributed to two forming bonds: one being the common carbon-copper bond, and other one is the oxygen-copper bond (Fig. 5d). As regards the *CO adsorption, only one carboncopper bond is identified, similar as for the Cu(111) surface (Fig. 5d).
Figure 5. DFT computation of CRR on various Cu-based catalysts. (a,b) Reaction pathways to CO and H2 on the surfaces of Cu(111), c-CuO(001), m-CuO(010), and CuOheterostructure(010) at 0 V vs RHE potential. (c) 2D activity volcano describing the limiting potential of CO2 to CO as a function of the *COOH and *CO free energy. Data for several other metal surfaces were taken from literature. The black line is a guide to eye showing scaling relationship. (d) Side view of *COOH and *CO adsorption configurations at the heterojunction of CuO-heterostructure.

sections.heading: Syngas Generation from Solar Energy
sections.text:
To simulate the real application of CO2 conversion, a twoelectrode cell was set up by applying RuO2-coated Ti electrode and free standing r-Cuox(350) membrane electrode as anode and cathode, respectively. As shown in Fig. 6a, the syngas starts to generate at a cell voltage of 1.6 V (without iR-free correction) and can reach a current of 2.5 mA at a voltage of 2.2 V. Under such conditions, the syngas generation rate was ~7 µmol/min/gcatal with a H2/CO ratio of 2 (Fig. 6a, Fig. S20). This production ratio can last at least over 18 h (Fig. 6b,c, Fig. S21), showing the outstanding stability of both materials and generation rate. Similar to the three-electrode system, adjusting the cell voltage can also tune the H2/CO ratio in gas products (Fig. 6a inset). Ultimately, CRR powered by a renewable energy source such as the sun is ideal and desirable, which requires small enough CRR overpotential and high enough F.E. of products.42, 43, 44. sections.heading: Conclusions
sections.text:
In conclusion, the oxide-derived Cu electrocatalyst demonstrates the controllable syngas production via CO2 reduction with high energetic efficiency, high current density and outstanding stability. These features ultimately guarantee
a high rate of syngas generation driven by commercial solar cells. Analysis of energetics indicates that the exceptional activity originates from a unique heterostructure at the interface of highly strained and interpenetrated m-CuO and cCuO domains on the shell of Cu NWs. An enhanced *COOH adsorption on these sites breaks the inherent linear scaling relationship of a series of reaction intermediates’ adsorption energies normally present on the conventional metal surfaces. The tuning of heterostructure to break the scaling relationship holds the promise to develop more efficient (electro)catalysts for broader applications. Also, combining highly efficient electrocatalysts for CO2 conversion with commercial renewable energy devices sheds light toward the next-generation syngas production.

sections.heading: Methods
sections.text:
Preparation of Cu NWs. Typically, NaOH (200 mL, 15 M), Cu(NO3)2 (10 mL, 0.1 M), ethylenediamine (EDA, 1.5 mL), and hydrazine (0.75 mL, 35 wt. %) were added to a 500 mL round bottom flask. The mixture was shaken by hand for 15 seconds
then heated at 80 ˚C and stirred at 180 rpm for approximately 45 minutes. Afterwards, Cu NWs were formed and floated to the top of solution. After washing with distilled water and ethanol several times, Cu NWs were collected.
Fabrication of the freestanding CuNW membrane electrode for CO2 reduction. A certain volume of the CuNW aqueous dispersion was filtered under reduced pressure within 5 min to form the freestanding membrane with the dimension of 1.8 cm. Afterwards, the CuNW membrane was subject to air oxidation in a tubular furnace under static air conditions for 4 days and then was annealed at different temperatures (from 300 to 400 °C) for 1.5 h. Before test, the oxidized CuNW membrane was electrochemically reduced at -1.3 V in N2-satuated KHCO3 electrolyte and then directly used as cathode for CO2 reduction. The reduced catalysts were characterized immediately and stored in a vacuum bag to avoid air oxidation.
Physicochemical characterization. Scanning electron microscopy (SEM) images were obtained by a field emission scanning electron microanalyzer (JEOL-6700F). X-ray diffraction (XRD) patterns were obtained by an XD-3 X-ray diffractometer. An X-ray photoelectron spectrometer (ESCALab MKII) was used to obtain the X-ray photoelectron spectroscopic (XPS) spectra. The XAS spectra were recorded in transmission mode (Si 111) at the BL14W1 End station of Shanghai Synchrotron Radiation Facility (SSRF). The electron beam energy of the storage ring was 3.5 GeV with a maximum stored current of 300 mA. The data were normalized and analyzed using Athena. Low resolution transmission electron microscopy (TEM) was conducted on a FEI Tecnai-G2 at an acceleration voltage of 120 kV. High-angle annular dark-field- scanning transmission electron microscopy (HAADF-STEM) images were recorded by a FEI Titan G2 60-300 microscope equipped with a Cs probe corrector at 300 kV.
Electrocatalytic activities of the membrane electrodes for CO2 reduction. Both three-electrode and two-electrode systems were used to measure the electrocatalytic CO2 reduction activity of different membrane electrodes. All the electrochemical experiments were performed in a H-type electrochemical cell with two compartments separated by a Nafion117 membrane.2,3 Each compartment had 50 mL of electrolyte (0.1 M KHCO3) and around 50 mL headspace. The measurements were carried out using a CHI760D electrochemical workstation at room temperature. In a conventional three-electrode system, a Pt plate and an Ag/AgCl in saturated KCl were used as counter and reference electrodes, respectively. The in-situ reduced freestanding CuNW membrane was directly used as a working electrode. In the twoelectrode system, the CuNW membrane and RuO2-coated Ti electrode were directly used as cathode and anode, respectively. Before test, the cathodic compartment of the cell was degassed and saturated with high-purity CO2 (99.9999%, BOC Gas) at 40 mL/min for at least 20 min. During the reduction process, CO2 gas was continuously bubbled into the cathodic chamber at a rate of 40 mL/min. All potentials were tested

Determination of samples. The gas samples were delivered directly to the sampling loop of an on-line gas chromatograph (GC) equipped with two channels. At the first analysis cycle, CO and CH4 were detected by Porapak Q and TDX-01 columns with a flame ionization detector (FID); H2 and CO2 were detected by TDX-01 column with a thermal conductivity detector (TCD) using Ar as a carrier gas. At the second analysis cycle, CH4, C2H4, C2H6 and C2H2 were detected by a Propark N column with a FID detector. The liquid products were measured by nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR, Bruker 400 MHz).
Computation Methods and Models. Spin polarized electronic structure calculations were carried out by DFT framework with the Perdew-Burke-Ernzerhof (PBE) exchange-correlation functional using a projector augmented-wave method in the VASP code.45, 46, 47, 48 For the plane-wave expansion, a 550 eV kinetic energy cut-off was used after testing a series of different energy values. The convergence criterion for electronic structure iteration was set to be 10-5 eV and that for geometry optimization was set to be 0.01 eV/Å. For large supercell computations, the convergence criterion was set to be 5 × 10-5 eV for electronic structure and 0.05 eV/Å for geometry. A Gaussian smearing of 0.20 eV was applied during the geometry optimization and for the total energy computation. The K-points were set to be 3 × 3 × 1 for Cu(111), 4 × 4 × 1 for cubic-CuO(001), 2 × 2 × 1 for monoclinic-CuO(010), and 1 × 3 × 1 CuOheterostructure(010), all using Monkhorst-pack grids except for the monoclinic structure, which used Gamma centred grids. Detailed model parameters are provided in supporting information. The Tkatchenko-Scheffler method was applied during all calculations to properly address the van der Waals interactions between atoms.
Free Energy Diagram Computation. The computational hydrogen electrode (CHE) model was applied to define the energy of a proton-electron pair at 0V vs RHE, which is ½ of the H2 free energy at 101,325 Pa. The free energy diagrams are all plotted under this electrode potential. The free energy of adsorbed *COOH, *CO, and *H were obtained by G = E + ZPE + ∫CpdT – TS where E is the DFT derived total energy of a system. Zero point energies (ZPE), enthalpic temperature correction (∫CpdT) and entropy correction (TS) were calculated on the basis of frequency analysis on the Cu(111) surface at room temperature 298.15 K (Table S3). During this process, frequencies were calculated by treating all 3N degrees of the adsorbates as vibrational in the harmonic oscillator approximation, and assuming that any changes in the vibrations of the substrate surface were minimal. The adsorbate solvation effects were included approximately in the same manner as in previous studies: *COOH was stabilized by 0.25 eV, *CO was stabilized by 0.10 eV.15 Gas-phase free energies were obtained by standard methods as well (Table S4). The standard state pressure of 101,325 Pa was used for the fugacity of gaseous species (CO2,
and CO); while a fugacity of 3534 Pa and 19 Pa were used for H2O, and HCOOH, respectively.1, 15 Gas phase energetics of species containing a CO backbone were compensated to match experimental values, namely 0.19 eV compensation for CO2, - 0.30 eV for CO, and 0.15 eV compensation for HCOOH.2
